أكتوبر 2026 – هوت العملة المحلية في السودان إلى مستويات غير مسبوقة، حيث تجاوز سعر الدولار الواحد حاجز 10 آلاف جنيه، وسط شح المعروض من النقد الأجنبي مقابل زيادة الطلب. ويشهد الجنيه السوداني منذ أسابيع تراجعًا ملحوظًا أمام العملات الأجنبية، ما انعكس على ارتفاع أسعار السلع الأساسية والخدمات، وفاقم الأعباء المعيشية على المواطنين. وقال متعاملون لـ “سودان تربيون”، الأربعاء، إن الجنيه عاود رحلة التراجع “حيث جرى تداول الدولار الواحد عند 10,105 جنيهات، والريال السعودي عند 2,645 جنيهًا للبيع، والجنيه المصري عند 190 جنيهًا، فيما بلغ سعر بيع الدرهم الإماراتي 2,750 جنيهًا، واليورو 11,320 جنيهًا” وأرجع المتعاملون تراجع الجنيه إلى زيادة الطلب على العملات الأجنبية، خاصة من جانب المستوردين وشركات الوقود، في ظل غياب حلول اقتصادية حقيقية لمعالجة الاختلالات في سوق النقد الأجنبي. وقال أحد المتعاملين إن السوق يشهد طلبًا متزايدًا على العملات الأجنبية من مختلف الفئات، بما في ذلك الراغبون في الحفاظ على مدخراتهم في ظل التراجع المستمر لقيمة العملة المحلية. وذكر أن الجهات المسؤولة تلجأ، عند مواجهة الأزمات، إلى زيادة الرسوم الجمركية والضرائب والجبايات، بدلًا من البحث عن حلول جذرية للأوضاع الاقتصادية، معتبرًا أن هذه السياسات فاقمت مشكلة شح النقد الأجنبي. ويأتي تجدد تراجع الجنيه السوداني في وقت يواجه فيه سوق النقد الأجنبي ضغوطًا متزايدة بفعل ارتفاع الطلب على العملات الصعبة، خصوصًا لتغطية احتياجات قطاع الوقود، بالتزامن مع استمرار التقلبات في أسعار الذهب، الذي يُعد أحد أهم مصادر النقد الأجنبي في البلاد. السريع في الفاشر الخرطوم 21 أكتوبر 2026 – طالبت نقابة الصحفيين السودانيين، الأربعاء، قوات الدعم السريع بالإفراج الفوري عن الصحفيين مصطفى فضل المولى ومعمر إبراهيم، والكشف عن مصير 4 صحفيين لا يزالون في عداد المختفين قسريًا. وفي مايو الماضي، قالت النقابة إن الصحفي معمر إبراهيم يعاني تدهورًا صحيًا خطيرًا داخل أحد معتقلات قوات الدعم السريع في مدينة نيالا بولاية جنوب دارفور، مشيرة إلى حرمانه من الرعاية الطبية. وقالت النقابة، في بيان، إن “فضل المولى محتجز لدى قوات الدعم السريع منذ سبتمبر 2023، دون توافر معلومات عن مكان احتجازه أو ظروفه، أو تمكّن أسرته من التواصل معه”. وأشارت إلى أن الصحفي معمر إبراهيم لا يزال محتجزًا لدى قوات الدعم السريع منذ أكتوبر 2025، في ظروف مجهولة، مع عدم السماح لأسرته بالتواصل معه. وطالبت بإطلاق سراح الصحفيين فورًا ودون قيد أو شرط، مضيفة أن استهداف الصحفيين يقوض حرية الصحافة وحق المجتمع في المعرفة، ويحد من تداول المعلومات والآراء، ويزيد صعوبة الوصول إلى الحقيقة في ظل النزاع المستمر. وأعربت النقابة عن قلقها إزاء الأوضاع الصحية والنفسية للصحفيين، في ظل تدهور البيئة الصحية وغياب الرعاية الطبية داخل معتقلات قوات الدعم السريع. وذكر البيان أن 4 صحفيين لا يزالون مختفين قسريًا. وحذرت النقابة من أن استمرار اختفاء الصحفيين في ظل الحرب، وما يصاحبها من عنف وخطاب كراهية وتحريض وانتشار للمعلومات المضللة، يزيد المخاطر التي تهدد حياتهم وسلامتهم النفسية، ويهيئ بيئة للإفلات من العقاب واستمرار الانتهاكات. وتقول منظمات معنية بحرية الصحافة إن الاعتقالات والاختفاء القسري وسوء المعاملة تمثل تهديدًا لسلامة الصحفيين، وتحد من قدرتهم على نقل المعلومات وتوثيق الانتهاكات خلال النزاعات المسلحة. ودعت النقابة الأمم المتحدة والمنظمات الدولية والإقليمية المعنية بحقوق الإنسان وحرية الصحافة إلى التحرك العاجل للكشف عن مصير الصحفيين المختفين، والضغط على أطراف النزاع لضمان سلامتهم والإفراج عنهم، ومحاسبة المسؤولين عن الانتهاكات. وتعرض صحفيون وعاملون في المجال الإعلامي بالسودان للاعتقال والاختفاء القسري منذ اندلاع الحرب بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع في أبريل 2023، وسط مخاوف متكررة بشأن سلامتهم وظروف احتجازهم. الكلمات: اعتقالات الإخفاء القسري نقابة الصحفيين السودانيين مقالات sudan.summary: احتل السودان المرتبة 138 من أصل 143 دولة في مؤشر سيادة القانون لعام 2026 الصادر عن مشروع العدالة العالمي (WJP). يشير التقرير إلى تدهور مستمر في سيادة القانون في البلاد، حيث انخفضت درجة السودان بنسبة 2.8% مقارنة بالعام السابق. على الصعيد الإقليمي، يحتل السودان المرتبة الأخيرة بين 34 دولة في أفريقيا جنوب الصحراء الكبرى. يعكس المؤشر تزايد التدخل الحكومي وتراجع الحريات الأساسية مثل حرية التعبير والتجمع. كما أظهر أن 62% من الدول شهدت تراجعًا في سيادة القانون، مما يعكس اتجاهاً عالمياً نحو الاستبداد. في المقابل، سجلت بعض التحسينات في إمكانية الوصول إلى العدالة المدنية، لكن السودان لا يزال يعاني من ضعف في العديد من المجالات المتعلقة بالحقوق الأساسية والشفافية الحكومية.

الحكومية للتنمية في شرق أفريقيا " إيغاد " و الاتحاد الأوروبي و مجلس الأمن يجسد فرضية أن "كثرة الطباخين تفسد الطبخة". تجاوز عثرات الماضي من جهتها، ترى المستشارة السابقة للمبعوث الأمريكي الخاص بالسودان، السفيرة سوزان بيج، أن جنيف حاولت تجاوز عثرات اللقاءات الخمسة السابقة (نواكشوط، القاهرة، بروكسل، نيويورك، جيبوتي) بالانتقال من هدن قصيرة إلى إطار زمني ملزم يؤسس لانتقال مدني وقوات مراقبة من "إيغاد" والاتحاد الأفريقي. إعلان لكن بيج تقر بصعوبة التطبيق جراء تضارب مصالح الدول الأعضاء، مشيرة إلى أن أوراق الضغط لن تثمر "ما لم تُمارس بصرامة على أطراف مثل السعودية والإمارات ومصر"، وسط تشابك إقليمي يشمل ملف سد النهضة الإثيوبي ومزاعم استخدام الأراضي لشن هجمات بالمسيّرات. ويتقاطع ذلك مع تنبيه الشرقاوي إلى خروج الأزمة السودانية من دائرة الأولويات الخمس الأولى لإدارة الرئيس الأمريكي دونالد ترمب ، منتقدا البيان الختامي لاكتفائه بالإقرار بالأمر الواقع المتمثل في عسكرة الصراع دون وضع صيغة سياسية حقيقية. 26 دولة ومنظمة شاركت في اجتماع جنيف بشأن السودان برعاية أممية (رويترز) معادلة صفرية ميدانيا وإنسانيا، يشدد تورشين على أن البندقية تظل الموجه الأساسي للمفاوضات؛ فالصراع يمثل "معادلة صفرية" تصطدم بكون الدعم السريع تشكيلا غير دستوري، مما يجعل اشتراطات الجيش للدمج والتسريح مستحيلة التحقق دون تفوق عسكري. ويتفاقم هذا الانسداد -وفق تورشين- مع عجز المجتمع الدولي عن فك الحصار عن الخرطوم و الفاشر (عاصمة شمال دارفور)، إثر عرقلة الدعم السريع اتفاقات إيصال المساعدات، وتراجع الالتزامات المالية الأمريكية، الأمر الذي أوقع الأمم المتحدة في عجز مالي حاد حال دون تغطية خطة الاستجابة الإنسانية البالغة 2.6 مليار دولار. ومنذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، تدور حرب طاحنة في السودان بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع، خلّفت عشرات آلاف بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية الرأي من بشريات أكتوبر 2020 إلى السقوط الحر في أكتوبر 2026 الرأي من بشريات أكتوبر 2020 إلى السقوط الحر في أكتوبر 2026 21 أكتوبر 2026 في الرأي 0 صورة تعبيرية د. سليمان علي أين كنا وأين وصلنا؟ ستة أعوام بين الأمل الذي كان يطرق أبواب السودان، وبين الواقع الذي يطرق أبواب السودانيين بالفقر والعجز وفقدان اليقين الوطني. في العشرين من أكتوبر 2020، كتبنا ونحن نستقبل ذكرى الحادي والعشرين من أكتوبر، وكنا نرى في الأفق ملامح وطن يلتقط أنفاسه بعد عقود من الاختناق والحصار والعقوبات الدولية. ↔️ كان الانتقال منصة جديدة للبناء القومي:_ كان السودان يومها يخطو خطواته الأولى في مرحلة انتقالية مثقلة بالتحديات، لكنه كان يمتلك شيئًا جوهريًا: الأمل في أن تكون الثورة بداية لتأسيس دولة جديدة، وأن تتحول تضحيات الشهداء إلى واقع يلمسه الناس في معاشهم وحريتهم وكرامتهم. كانت كلمات ذلك اليوم تحمل شيئًا من نشوة الانتصار؛ «يا أكتوبر الأرض تغني وباسمك الشعب انتصر، وحائط السجن انكسر». وكانت إزالة اسم السودان من قائمة الدول الراعية للإرهاب إحدى العلامات البارزة التي استقبل بها السودانيون تلك المرحلة، باعتبارها نافذة للخروج من العزلة الدولية، واستعادة العلاقات الاقتصادية والمالية، وفتح الطريق أمام فرص جديدة للتعافي وإعادة بناء الدولة. لم يكن السودان في عام 2020 دولة مكتملة العافية، ولم تكن أحوال الناس الاقتصادية مثالية، بل كانت الأزمات المعيشية والتضخم واختلالات الاقتصاد حاضرة بقوة. لكن الفارق أن البلاد كانت لديها فرصة سياسية للانتقال، وتوقعات بإصلاح المؤسسات، واستعادة الإنتاج، وبناء اقتصاد يخدم المواطنين بدلًا من أن يكون عبئًا إضافيًا على حياتهم. أما اليوم، في أكتوبر 2026، فالسؤال الذي يفرض نفسه كيف وصلنا إلى هنا؟ ستة أعوام كانت كافية لتكشف المسافة الهائلة بين الوعود التي حملتها المرحلة الانتقالية، والواقع الذي انتهى إليه السودان. تدهورت الحالة الوطنية إلى مستوى سحيق، وتآكلت القدرة الشرائية للعملة إلى حد باتت معه الدخول التي كانت توفر الحد الأدنى من متطلبات الحياة عاجزة عن ملاحقة الأسعار. فقد الناس قيمة جهدهم وعرقهم، وأصبحت المرتبات أرقامًا على الورق، لا تعكس قدرة حقيقية على توفير الغذاء والدواء والسكن والتعليم. لم تعد الأزمة مجرد ارتفاع في الأسعار، ولا مجرد انخفاض في سعر العملة. إنها أزمة اقتصاد فقد قدرته على حماية قيمة العمل، وأزمة دولة تراجعت قدرتها على تنظيم النشاط الاقتصادي وتوفير الخدمات وضمان الحد الأدنى من الاستقرار. حين يعمل الإنسان شهرًا كاملًا ثم يكتشف أن ما يتقاضاه لا يكفي احتياجات أسرته الأساسية، فإن الخلل يتجاوز ميزانية الأسرة إلى بنية الاقتصاد والسياسات التي تحكمه. وفي الوقت الذي كان يفترض أن تتجه فيه البلاد إلى توسيع الإنتاج الزراعي والصناعي، وتطوير البنية التحتية، وتهيئة بيئة الاستثمار، اتسعت دائرة الفشل والانكماش الاقتصادي، وتراجعت قدرات قطاعات واسعة على العمل والإنتاج. وأصبح نشاط المضاربات في الأراضي والعملات، في ظل اختلالات السوق وانعدام الاستقرار، ملاذًا لبعض رؤوس الأموال، بينما تحمل المنتجون والمزارعون والعمال وأصحاب الأعمال الصغيرة كلفة الانهيار. ↔️ الحرب وعوامل سابقة لها تتحمل ما يجري الان؟ لقد انتقل السودان من سؤال كيفية استثمار الفرصة التي أتاحها الانفتاح الدولي؟ ، إلى سؤال كيفية حماية ما تبقى من مقومات الحياة؟. وبين السؤالين ضاعت سنوات ثمينة، وتراكمت الأزمات، وانفتح الباب أمام حرب مدمرة لم تكتفِ بإيقاف مسار الانتقال، بل ألحقت أضرارًا واسعة بالمؤسسات والأسواق وسبل العيش، ودفعت ملايين السودانيين إلى النزوح واللجوء وفقدان مصادر دخلهم. ومع ذلك، فإن اختزال كل ما حدث في الحرب وحدها لا يقدم تفسيرًا كاملًا للمأساة. فالحرب كانت عاملًا مدمرًا ومسرّعًا للانهيار، لكنها جاءت فوق أرضية من هشاشة المؤسسات، وأزمة الحكم، وضعف بناء التوافق الوطني، وتعثر الإصلاح الاقتصادي، وعجز القوى السياسية عن تحويل شعارات الثورة إلى مشروع دولة تتجاوز صراعات السلطة ومصالح الجماعات. هنا تكمن المأساة الحقيقية: لم تكن المشكلة في غياب الموارد، فالسودان بلد واسع الإمكانات الزراعية والحيوانية والمعدنية، ويمتلك موقعًا جغرافيًا استراتيجيًا وموارد بشرية قادرة على الإسهام في نهضته. وإنما كانت المشكلة، ولا تزال، في كيفية إدارة هذه الموارد، وفي طبيعة السلطة التي تتحكم فيها، وفي غياب مشروع وطني يجعل الإنتاج أولوية، ويضع مصالح المواطنين فوق حسابات التمكين والاحتكار والصراع. أين كنا وأين وصلنا؟ كان السودان في أكتوبر 2020 يتطلع إلى كسر العزلة، واستعادة موقعه في المجتمع الدولي، وفتح الطريق أمام التعافي الاقتصادي. أما في أكتوبر 2026، فإن السودانيين يواجهون تحديات البقاء، ويبحثون عن الأمن والغذاء والدواء ومصادر الرزق، بينما يحتاج الوطن إلى إعادة بناء ما دمرته الحرب، وإصلاح ما أفسدته سنوات الاختلال السياسي والاقتصادي. كان الأمل أن تنكسر جدران العزلة، وأن تتسع أمام البلاد أبواب المستقبل. لكن ما حدث أن جدرانًا أخرى ارتفعت: جدران الحرب، والانقسام، والفقر، وانعدام الثقة، وتراجع القدرة على الحلم. ولعل أكثر ما يستحق المراجعة اليوم هو أن إزالة اسم السودان من قائمة الدول الراعية للإرهاب لم تكن، في حد ذاتها، مشروعًا للنهضة، بل كانت فرصة تحتاج إلى رؤية اقتصادية، واستقرار سياسي، ومؤسسات قادرة على تحويل الانفتاح الدولي إلى إنتاج وفرص عمل وتحسن في مستوى المعيشة. فالانفتاح لا يبني دولة بمفرده، ورفع القيود لا يعوض غياب السياسات، كما أن الشعارات الثورية لا تغني عن بناء المؤسسات. ↔️ كيف نضع الوطن في منصة انطلاق جديدة؟ إن استعادة الوطن، تحتاج إلى مشروع وطني طموح يعيد تعريف أولويات الدولة: حماية الإنسان، واستعادة المؤسسات، وإحياء الإنتاج، وإصلاح النظام المالي، وإعادة بناء الخدمات، وتوزيع السلطة والثروة بعدالة، وتأسيس حكم يستمد شرعيته من المواطنين وقدرته على خدمتهم. وتحتاج هذه المهمة إلى مراجعة شجاعة لتجربة السنوات الماضية، لا بهدف تبادل الاتهامات أو تصفية الحسابات، وإنما لتحديد المسؤوليات ولفهم كيف تحولت فرصة تاريخية إلى مأساة وطنية، ولماذا عجزت القوى التي رفعت شعارات التغيير عن حماية المسار الذي بشرت به، وكيف تقدمت حسابات السلطة على مطلوبات حماية الثورة والانتقال الديمقراطي وبناء دولة كل السودانيين. أكتوبر ليس مجرد ذكرى في التقويم السياسي السوداني، ولا أغنية تستعاد كل عام، بل هو سؤال متجدد عن معنى الثورة، وعن العلاقة بين تضحيات الشعب والنتائج التي يجنيها. وإذا كانت أكتوبر 1964 قد حملت وعدًا بالخلاص من الاستبداد، وكانت ديسمبر 2018 تعبيرًا عن تطلع جيل جديد إلى الحرية والسلام والعدالة، فإن مسؤوليتنا اليوم أن نمنع تحول هذه التضحيات إلى مجرد صفحات في تاريخ وطن أضاع فرصه. أين كانت البلد وأين وصلت؟ كان الحلم أن ينتقل السودان من العزلة إلى الانفتاح، ومن الاستبداد إلى الحكم المدني، ومن اقتصاد الأزمات إلى اقتصاد الإنتاج. واليوم، بعد ستة أعوام، نقف أمام سؤال أشد إيلامًا: كيف نحول ما تبقى من الوطن إلى بداية جديدة؟ ، بدلًا من أن نترك الانهيار يكتب خاتمة الحلم؟ إن السودان لا يحتاج إلى استعادة صور أكتوبر 2020 وحدها، بل إلى استعادة المعنى الذي جعل السودانيين يؤمنون بأن التغيير ممكن. يحتاج إلى دولة لا تهدر قيمة العمل، ولا تبدد الموارد، ولا تجعل المواطن يدفع ثمن فشل النخب وصراعاتها. يحتاج إلى مشروع وطني يتجاوز الحرب، ويؤسس لسلام مستدام، واقتصاد منتج، وعدالة في توزيع السلطة والثروة، ومؤسسات تحمي الجميع دون استثناء. فالمجد للشهداء لا يكون بترديد أسمائهم فحسب، وإنما ببناء الوطن الذي استشهدوا من أجله. والتقدم لا يقاس بما نعلنه من انتصارات، بل بما يستعيده المواطن من أمن وكرامة وقدرة على العيش. أكتوبر الذي غنّى له السودان بالأمس، يجب أن يكون اليوم مناسبة لمراجعة المسار، ومواجهة الحقيقة، واستعادة الوطن من قبضة الحرب والفشل والانقسام. فالسؤال الجوهري اليوم: هل نملك الإرادة لبناء سودان جديد؟ ، أم سنظل نستهلك ذكريات الانتصارات بينما تتآكل مقومات الحياة أمام أعيننا؟ مقالات ذات صلة نقد: للدولار الواحد هذا الأسبوع. ومع استمرار الحرب، خفض السودان إنتاج قطاعات تعد من المصادر الرئيسية للدولار، في حين يتزايد تهريب الذهب إلى الخارج، وهو ‌أهم سلعة تصدرها البلاد. وفي الوقت نفسه، قالت الحكومة البرهان الخرطوم 21 أكتوبر 2026 – أصدر رئيس مجلس السيادة الانتقالي، الفريق أول ركن عبد الفتاح البرهان، قراراً بإعادة المؤسسة السودانية للنفط، بعد سبع سنوات من حلها. وتضطلع المؤسسة بدور استراتيجي في تنمية الثروة النفطية وحسن استغلالها، من خلال أعمال الاستكشاف والإنتاج، فضلاً عن توفير احتياجات البلاد من المواد البترولية المختلفة وتأمين المخزون الاستراتيجي. وَقال بيان صحفي لوزارة الطاقة والنفط الأربعاء إن رئيس مجلس السيادة عبد الفتاح البرهان أصدر قراراً بإعادة “المؤسسة السودانية للنفط”، بعد سبع سنوات من حلها في العام 2019. وجاء القرار في إطار جهود الدولة لإصلاح وإعادة تنظيم قطاع الطاقة وتفعيل قانون الثروة النفطية وإعادة تكوين مجلس النفط برئاسة رئيس مجلس السيادة، ويضم في عضويته قيادات عليا وجهات اختصاص سيادية واقتصادية وأمنية. ويضم مجلس النفط وزراء النفط والمالية والعدل، ومدير جهاز المخابرات العامة، ورئيس جهاز الاستثمار الوطني، إلى جانب عدد محدود من خبراء النفط، بما يجمع الجهات السيادية والاقتصادية والفنية ذات الصلة بالقطاع. وفي السياق ذاته، أصدر البرهان قراراً بتعيين اللواء بحري المتقاعد الدكتور إسماعيل عثمان الحسين أبوشوك أميناً عاماً للمؤسسة السودانية للنفط. وكان بنك السودان المركزي وافق، في ديسمبر 2025، على تعيين أبوشوك مديراً عاماً لبنك النيلين المملوك للدولة، غير أن القرار أثار جدلاً في الأوساط الاقتصادية والمصرفية بشأن مدى صلته بالقطاع المصرفي، الذي يتطلب تولي قياداته خبرات متخصصة. واعتذر أبوشوك لاحقاً عن تولي المنصب، عقب انتقادات لتعيين عسكريين متقاعدين في إدارة البنوك والمصارف. وتدرج أبوشوك في الرتب العسكرية منذ تخرجه في الدفعة 29، حتى وصل إلى رتبة لواء قبل إحالته إلى التقاعد، كما حصل أثناء الخدمة على درجة الدكتوراه في مجال العلوم العسكرية البحرية. وفي سبتمبر 2023، تقدم أبوشوك، ضمن مجموعة من الضباط المتقاعدين، بمذكرة إلى رئيس مجلس السيادة والقائد العام للقوات المسلحة، عبد الفتاح البرهان، أعلنوا فيها تأييدهم لتفويضه بالقضاء على قوات الدعم السريع والاستمرار في الدفاع عن حقوق المواطنين. وأُنشئت المؤسسة السودانية للنفط بموجب قانون الثروة النفطية لعام 1998، بوصفها مؤسسة عامة تتمتع بشخصية اعتبارية مستقلة، ويقع مقرها في الخرطوم. وكانت تخضع لسلطات مجلس النفط، الذي كان يرأسه رئيس الجمهورية، تحت إشراف وزير النفط، قبل أن تُحل في عام 2019. مقالات ذات صلة والي وسط دارفور ينتقل بحكومته إلى (روكرو) بأعالي جبل مرة وفاة مانديلا ترجئ مفاوضات الحكومة Attending Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations as President William Ruto’s guest of honour, Abiy emphasized the longstanding partnership between the two countries, highlighting cooperation in electricity, telecommunications, trade and regional connectivity. Yet beyond the diplomatic celebrations, the visit coincided with growing tensions involving Somalia, whose internal political crisis has begun complicating its relations with both Ethiopia and Kenya. Although Abiy’s visit was officially centered on Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations and bilateral cooperation, it unfolded against a backdrop of growing regional tensions involving Somalia. The visit did not publicly establish a common Ethiopian and Kenyan position on the Somali crisis, but it brought renewed attention to the strategic importance of their partnership as both countries navigate increasingly complicated relations with Mogadishu. The significance of Ethiopia’s relationship with Kenya extends beyond bilateral cooperation. Both countries have invested considerable military and diplomatic resources in Somalia’s stabilization, particularly in efforts to contain Al Shabaab and prevent insecurity from spreading across their borders. However, Somalia’s confrontation between its federal government and regional political actors is creating disagreements over the responsibilities of neighbouring countries. For Ethiopia, the challenge is to maintain its commitment to Somalia’s security without becoming involved in political disputes that could undermine its wider regional interests. The immediate source of tension lies in Somalia’s South West State, where the removal of former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in March 2026 failed to produce a lasting political settlement. Instead, confrontations between his supporters and forces aligned with the federal government have continued, exposing deeper disagreements over regional autonomy and the distribution of political authority. By October 19, forces loyal to Laftagareen reportedly controlled five towns in the Bay region, including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere and Dinsoor, complicating Mogadishu’s efforts to consolidate authority. The conflict is particularly consequential because the South West State includes territories where Ethiopian forces have maintained a security presence for years. According to Somali Guardian reporting published on October 19 , Somali federal authorities requested Ethiopian military assistance against forces aligned with Laftagareen, but Ethiopian commanders declined to participate in what they considered an internal political confrontation. Although the reported exchange has not been independently confirmed, it illustrates a fundamental question concerning foreign military involvement in Somalia: whether security assistance intended to confront common threats should extend to supporting the federal government in disputes over domestic political authority. For Ethiopia, the issue has acquired additional importance following the transition from the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia, ATMIS, to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM, which commenced on January 1, 2025. Under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2767 , the successor mission was authorized to support Somali forces against Al Shabaab, protect civilians and facilitate the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali institutions. Its mandate also encompasses security support for political processes, but does not provide unrestricted authority to determine the outcome of internal political disputes. The transition brought renewed attention to the distinction between Ethiopian troops operating under African Union arrangements and those deployed through separate bilateral security understandings. This distinction matters because forces assigned to AUSSOM operate within a defined multinational framework, while deployments outside that structure depend on separate arrangements with Somalia. In its December 2025 communiqué , the African Union Peace and Security Council explicitly acknowledged Ethiopia and Uganda for deploying additional troops under bilateral arrangements. Their presence cannot therefore be understood solely through AUSSOM’s command structure. Ethiopia’s longstanding involvement in Somalia has primarily been driven by the need to prevent Al Shabaab from developing secure operating areas near Ethiopian territory. The group’s ability to exploit instability and threaten communities across borders makes developments in Somalia directly relevant to Ethiopia’s national security. Ethiopian military operations and participation in successive African Union missions have consequently contributed to a broader effort to contain threats before they reach Ethiopian territory. The South West State remains especially important because the Bay and Bakool regions form part of the wider security environment connected to Ethiopia’s eastern frontier. Participation in Somalia’s internal political confrontations, however, would expose Ethiopia to different risks. Military intervention could associate Ethiopian forces with one Somali political faction, weaken relationships with local communities and transform a defined security commitment into an extended responsibility for political outcomes. Even a successful intervention would not necessarily resolve disagreements concerning federal authority and regional political representation. Somalia’s domestic disputes require political settlements that military involvement by neighbouring countries cannot independently deliver. This position should not be confused with opposition to Somalia’s federal government. Addis Ababa and Mogadishu continue to maintain diplomatic relations and share an interest in preventing renewed militant expansion. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s September 29 visit to Addis Ababa , during which he discussed bilateral relations and regional security with Abiy Ahmed, demonstrated the continued importance of diplomatic engagement despite existing disagreements. Those disagreements nevertheless have a deeper history. The January 2024 memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland, which addressed potential Ethiopian maritime access, produced a significant confrontation with Mogadishu over sovereignty and territorial integrity. Somalia regarded the arrangement as an infringement on its sovereignty, while Ethiopia viewed access to the sea as an important strategic and economic objective. The dispute contributed to Somalia’s closer security engagement with Egypt, which already maintained long winded Nile disagreements with Ethiopia. The December 2024 Ankara Declaration , facilitated by Türkiye, helped restore diplomatic engagement by reaffirming mutual respect for sovereignty and acknowledging the possibility of mutually beneficial maritime arrangements under Somalia’s sovereign authority. Nevertheless, restoring diplomatic communication did not eliminate competing regional security calculations. Egypt’s expanding security engagement with Somalia and its prospective contribution to AUSSOM have introduced further sensitivity into discussions about troop deployments. The African Union’s June 2025 negotiations with troop-contributing countries included Ethiopia and Egypt, demonstrating that both countries were considered within the mission’s institutional arrangements. In December 2025, the African Union also acknowledged Egypt’s preparations for deployment while emphasizing the need to prevent security gaps during the transition. Political endorsement, negotiated contributions and actual troop deployments, however, remain distinct stages. For Ethiopia, any substantial expansion of Egyptian forces near areas where Ethiopian troops operate would raise operational questions, particularly given the unresolved Nile dispute. Careful coordination would be essential to prevent competing strategic interests from complicating counterterrorism operations. Kenya faces a related challenge arising from Somalia’s domestic political confrontation. Laftagareen’s presence in Kenya following his removal has generated criticism from Somali officials. On October 19, Somalia’s parliamentary speaker, Abdikadir Mohamed Nur Jama, reportedly accused individuals residing in Kenya of involvement in activities connected to the conflict and questioned the alleged protection they received. The reporting did not establish evidence supporting those allegations, and Kenyan authorities had not publicly responded at the time. Hosting Somali political figures does not independently demonstrate Kenyan government support for their military activities. Nairobi must balance its diplomatic responsibilities and continued cooperation with Mogadishu against its own legal and national security considerations. The consequences of Somali instability for Kenya are also economic. The Lamu Port South Sudan Ethiopia Transport corridor, LAPSSET, represents an important regional infrastructure initiative intended to expand commercial connectivity and diversify access to maritime trade. Its security is connected to conditions in northern and coastal Kenya, where Al Shabaab has demonstrated the ability to threaten personnel and transport infrastructure. On September 19, 2026, suspected militants attacked Kenyan military personnel patrolling part of the corridor in Garissa. No casualties were reported, but the incident illustrated the security demands associated with protecting strategic infrastructure. Although these attacks cannot be directly attributed to the South West State’s political crisis, prolonged instability in Somalia could place additional pressure on counterterrorism operations and create opportunities for militant expansion. For Kenya, preserving security cooperation with Somalia therefore carries implications for domestic security, investment and regional transport connectivity. Ethiopia shares an interest in protecting these connections, which could strengthen economic integration and provide additional commercial routes. Against this background, the partnership between Addis Ababa and Nairobi offers continuity. Cooperation in electricity transmission, telecommunications and transport has created practical interests that extend beyond individual political disagreements. During his October 20 visit , Abiy emphasized Ethiopia’s electricity exports to Kenya, Safaricom’s presence in Ethiopia and growing commercial connections. Their importance becomes greater as Ethiopia confronts renewed tensions with Eritrea, instability in northern Ethiopia and unresolved strategic disagreements with Egypt. The October 2026 escalation in Tigray and tensions with Eritrea demonstrate the competing pressures confronting Addis Ababa. Strong relations with Kenya provide an additional channel for diplomatic consultation without requiring both governments to adopt identical policies toward Somalia. The coming months will test whether the three countries can prevent Somalia’s internal confrontation from developing into a wider regional dispute. Particular attention should be given to the security situation around Baidoa, changes to Ethiopian and Egyptian troop arrangements, and Somalia’s political preparations ahead of the presidential election announced for May 15, 2027 . Diplomatic engagement through Kenya, IGAD or other regional mechanisms could become increasingly relevant if political divisions deepen. Whether mediation initiatives emerge, however, will depend on the willingness of the parties to pursue negotiation. Abiy’s Kenya visit ultimately illustrates the continuing value of dependable regional partnerships during a period of uncertainty. Ethiopia’s national interests require a stable Somalia, effective cooperation against Al Shabaab and security arrangements that do not unnecessarily entangle Ethiopian forces in domestic political rivalries. Its relationship with Kenya offers opportunities to advance those objectives while protecting economic integration and regional connectivity. The challenge for Addis Ababa is to preserve this partnership alongside constructive engagement with Mogadishu, ensuring that Somalia’s political disagreements do not become another source of confrontation across the Horn of Africa. A comparison of the IGAD facilitated process that produced the 1988 agreement with the Turkish brokered Ankara Declaration of December 2024 reveals both the continuity of Ethiopia’s core security interests and the shifting diplomatic environment in which those interests are pursued. The confrontation that shaped the 1980s negotiations originated in the aftermath of the 1977–78 Ogaden War. Somalia continued to assert territorial claims over the Ogaden region of Ethiopia. Mutual destabilization compounded by internal pressures on both regimes produced a protracted period of tension short of renewed full scale interstate war. At the inaugural IGAD summit in Djibouti in January 1986 Ethiopian leader Mengistu Haile Mariam and Somali President Siad Barre established a joint ad hoc ministerial committee to examine the sources of bilateral discord. Although the committee was formally joint Ethiopia’s representatives led at key sessions by Foreign Minister Lt-Col. Goshu Wolde consistently prioritized recognition of existing international boundaries and the cessation of support for anti Ethiopian groups. This agenda setting approach shaped the substance of the talks. Somalia preferred to sequence confidence building measures troop disengagement restoration of diplomatic relations and prisoner exchanges before addressing the boundary question. Three principal ministerial sessions took place in May 1986 August 1986 and April 1987. Progress remained limited because of these differing priorities. A further meeting between the two heads of state on the margins of the March 1988 IGAD summit in Djibouti provided the decisive political impetus. The resulting agreement formalized after talks in Mogadishu on 3 and 4 April 1988 restored diplomatic relations provided for the withdrawal of security forces from the border ended hostile propaganda terminated mutual support for insurgent groups and arranged the exchange of prisoners of war. Both sides agreed to discuss the boundary question at a later date. In practice the accord ended active Somali claims on the Ogaden and secured Ethiopia’s south eastern frontier freeing Ethiopian resources for pressing internal challenges. The 1988 agreement demonstrated that a regional structure could deliver tangible results when the parties shared a pragmatic interest in stabilizing a disputed border and when one party Ethiopia articulated its security requirements with clarity and consistency. No open interstate war between Ethiopia and Somalia occurred after 1988. Somalia’s subsequent state collapse created a different environment. Under Prime Minister Meles Zenawi Ethiopia engaged constructively in efforts to rebuild Somali institutions helping to shape the transitional federal structure that emerged in the absence of a functioning central authority. This engagement responded first to immediate security concerns arising from the political space along Ethiopia’s border. At the same time it reinforced Ethiopia’s standing as a constructive regional actor. When the Islamic Courts Union consolidated control over much of southern Somalia in 2006 and posed a direct security challenge Ethiopia intervened in support of the Transitional Federal Government. Limited deployments earlier that year preceded full scale action in December 2006. That intervention reflected continuity rather than rupture Ethiopia acted to prevent hostile forces from establishing themselves in adjacent ungoverned space. Serious bilateral tension re emerged only in 2024 following the January memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland concerning commercial and naval access to the sea. Somalia denounced the arrangement as a violation of its territorial integrity, recalled its ambassador and explicitly rejected African Union mediation efforts conditioning any engagement on Ethiopia’s retraction of the memorandum. This stance effectively limited the immediate scope for regional bodies including IGAD to facilitate dialogue on a dispute touching core sovereignty claims. The political climate had become more transactional with parties weighing concrete exchanges of interests rather than operating within the denser shared outlooks of earlier periods. The Ankara Declaration of 11–12 December 2024 facilitated by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, produced a de escalation. The leaders reaffirmed respect for each other’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. They acknowledged the potential benefits of Ethiopia’s assured access to and from the sea while affirming that any commercial arrangements would operate under the sovereign authority of the Federal Republic of Somalia. Technical negotiations were scheduled to begin no later than the end of February 2025 and to conclude within four months with Turkish facilitation available as needed. IGAD welcomed the declaration as a constructive step toward regional stability that external facilitation can complement rather than displace regional mechanisms when circumstances require additional diplomatic weight. In the mid 1980s member state cohesion a bipolar international context that channeled regional diplomacy and a shared interest in border stability enabled IGAD to serve as an effective vehicle. Ethiopia acting within that institutional framework advanced outcomes consistent with its security requirements. Three decades later protracted state fragility in Somalia internal challenges across several Horn countries and the proliferation of external actors with diverse interests altered the diplomacy. Regional organizations continue to perform important roles however on certain sovereignty laden disputes their immediate leverage may be constrained. Ethiopia’s posture has remained consistent across these decades safeguarding the south eastern frontier preventing the establishment of hostile actors in adjacent ungoverned spaces and securing reliable access to the sea. The instruments joint committees under a regional umbrella support for transitional governance calibrated military engagement when necessary and pragmatic external facilitation have adapted to changing conditions. In 2024 Turkish mediation filled a temporary institutional vacuum created by the particular constraints facing regional mechanisms on this sovereignty sensitive question. The 1988 accord and the 2024 Ankara Declaration both illustrate that durable progress depends less on the formal identity of the mediator than on the alignment of core interests and the availability of credible channels for dialogue. ethiopia.content: The Sodere Initiative and Ethiopia’s Role in Somali State-Building – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 The Sodere Initiative and Ethiopia’s Role in Somali State-Building 0 Comments Ethiopia’s initiative at Sodere brought Somalia’s rival factions into a common political process at a time when the country lacked a central authority capable of negotiating on its behalf. Convened in late 1996 under IGAD’s newly established conflict-resolution mandate, the talks culminated on 3 January 1997 in the creation of a 41-member National Salvation Council, with representation allocated to the four major clan families and smaller communities. Although Sodere did not produce a lasting government, it established a broad-based framework for political representation that subsequent reconciliation efforts would revisit The collapse of the Somali state in January 1991 left political authority dispersed among armed factions, while successive international efforts failed to establish a national government capable of consolidating control. The Addis Ababa Agreement of 1993 brought leading factions into a common framework, but agreement on paper did not resolve the struggle for power in Mogadishu; by the time the last United Nations troops withdrew in March 1995, the underlying competition remained intact. Rivalry between Ali Mahdi Mohamed and the Aideed camp, which passed to Hussein Aideed following General Mohamed Farah Aideed’s death in August 1996, continued to obstruct the emergence of a national political authority. The consequences extended beyond the capital. In the border region of Gedo, Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI) established a presence centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometers from Ethiopia, which Addis Ababa regarded as a base for a movement responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linked to other armed groups opposed to its government. Somalia’s fragmentation thus presented Ethiopia with a problem that international mediation alone had not resolved, the absence of a functioning state was not merely prolonging conflict within Somalia but also leaving neighboring territory exposed to armed networks that could operate across the border. This gave Ethiopia a direct security interest in the restoration of Somali political authority. The expansion of regional institutions in 1996 provided an important foundation for a more coordinated response to Somalia’s political fragmentation, creating a framework through which Ethiopia could address its security concerns while contributing to a regional effort to restore Somali political dialogue. Founded in 1986 as the Intergovernmental Authority on Drought and Development, with a mandate centred on drought and desertification, the organization was reconstituted as the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) following the amendment of its founding instrument in Nairobi on 21 March 1996 and its relaunch at the Djibouti summit of 25–26 November. The revised charter incorporated the prevention, management and resolution of inter-state and intra-state conflicts through dialogue, placing peace and security alongside food security and economic cooperation among the organization’s priorities. This change reflected a broader recognition that the conflicts confronting the Horn of Africa required regional mechanisms capable of addressing their political and security dimensions. For Ethiopia, whose border security was directly affected by the absence of effective authority in Somalia, IGAD’s expanded mandate offered a legitimate avenue for supporting reconciliation through regional diplomacy. The framework connected Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns with the wider regional interest in reducing conflict and restoring political order in Somalia, giving its diplomatic engagement an institutional foundation and a shared regional purpose. Although divisions among IGAD members, including the severance of relations with Sudan by Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda during the preceding year, complicated regional cooperation, the organization’s expanded mandate established an important basis for renewed engagement. OAU strengthened this framework in July 1996, when its Yaoundé resolution recognized Meles Zenawi, then outgoing OAU chairman, as holding a special mandate to facilitate peace in Somalia and supported efforts by IGAD member states to reactivate their initiatives. This endorsement connected the emerging regional effort to the OAU’s broader diplomatic role and reinforced the legitimacy of renewed attempts to bring Somali factions into negotiations. Ethiopia subsequently informed the United Nations Security Council that it had convened the Sodere conference in November 1996 in accordance with an IGAD mandate. Operating within this reinforced regional framework, Ethiopian conduct in the second half of 1996 ran along two tracks that differed in instrument yet converged through local partnerships. On the military track, Ethiopia acted against Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI), an Islamist group that had established a presence in the Gedo region centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Addis Ababa regarded AIAI as a direct security threat, holding it responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linking it to other armed networks opposed to the Ethiopian government. Ethiopian forces therefore crossed into Gedo on 9 August 1996 to attack AIAI bases, and fighting continued through December. The fourth major assault on the group, launched on 11 June 1997, captured Luuq and Buulo Haawo and deprived AIAI of its last major bases in the region. This military campaign ran in parallel with a political initiative that sought to harness Somali opposition to AIAI and embed Ethiopia’s border-security objectives within a broader reconciliation process. On the political track, Ethiopia convened Somali leaders at the Sodere resort for roughly six weeks of talks, which ended on 3 January 1997 with a declaration signed by 27 leaders representing 26 factions. The declaration created a National Salvation Council of 41 members and a National Executive Committee of 11 members led by five co-chairmen, with authority to speak for the Council and to prepare a Transitional Central Authority or Provisional Central Government, and it committed the signatories to a National Reconciliation Conference at Bossaso. The Somali National Front, a competitor of AIAI for control of Gedo, was among the signatories. That overlap offered Somali opponents of AIAI an institutional route to national standing and tied a border security objective to a political process that Somali actors could own. The composition of the Council contains the process’s most durable contribution. Nine seats went to each of the four major clan families, Darod, Hawiye, Rahanweyn and Dir, and five to smaller groups, a distribution that totals 41 and approximates the half-share later formalized for minorities under the 4.5 formula. For the first time the Darod accepted parity among the main clan families. That principle of clan-family parity, first given institutional expression at Sodere, was subsequently formalized at the Arta conference in 2000 and then applied at scale by the Mbagathi process, which in 2004 allocated 61 seats to each of the four major families and 31 to the minority bloc within a 275-member Transitional Federal Parliament. By converting a contest over who speaks for Somalia into a bounded negotiation over who sits within each family’s allotment, parity supplied the mechanism through which Sodere moved Somali politics from open military competition toward transitional institutions. Sodere’s significance extended beyond the representational framework it helped establish to the regional diplomacy through which that framework was pursued. Ethiopia’s subsequent involvement in Somali reconciliation formed part of a recurring pattern that included hosting the 1993 Addis Ababa conference, convening Sodere in 1996 and 1997, participating in the IGAD-mediated Mbagathi talks that produced the Transitional Federal Charter in 2004, and contributing troops to the African Union missions in Somalia, AMISOM and ATMIS, and now AUSSOM. The Mbagathi record offers particularly clear evidence that Somali actors themselves regarded Ethiopia’s participation as consequential. In February 2004, six faction leaders of the Somali Restoration and Reconstruction Council announced that they would stay out of the final phase of the talks while Ethiopia was absent from the table. Hussein Aideed, who had succeeded his father General Mohamed Farah Aideed in 1996 and had remained outside the Sodere process the following year, now argued that a regional peace process required consensus among neighbouring states as well as among Somalis. His position marked a shift from contesting Ethiopia’s involvement in 1997 to treating the participation of neighboring states as a condition of a credible settlement, illustrating how the regional approach embodied at Sodere became an established feature of subsequent Somali peace negotiations. This historical experience has direct relevance as Somalia confronts a demanding security transition, with Al-Shabaab continuing to threaten state consolidation, domestic political negotiations remaining unsettled after the inconclusive May 2026 talks, and AUSSOM’s operational future facing growing financial uncertainty following Washington’s announced intention to end its support for UN logistics and operations from 2027. Ethiopia’s renewed commitment to AUSSOM, reaffirmed at the August 2026 troop-contributing countries summit, provides an important basis for strengthening this regional security relationship. Somalia’s current security transition increases the strategic importance of sustained coordination with Ethiopia. Al-Shabaab retains a presence in areas of Gedo and Bakool near the Ethiopian frontier, while Washington’s decision to end funding for UN logistical support to AUSSOM after December 2026 adds pressure to the mission’s operational continuity. These developments connect Somalia’s internal security challenges directly to the management of its western border, where gaps in territorial control can enable armed groups to move, reorganize and exploit weaknesses in coordination between security forces. Ethiopia’s direct exposure to these threats, its existing security involvement in Somalia and its capacity to operate along the shared frontier make bilateral cooperation consequential to how these risks are managed. For Mogadishu, the practical priority is to establish predictable arrangements with Addis Ababa for intelligence exchange, border threat assessment, troop coordination and consultation over operations affecting Somali territory. These mechanisms would help align Ethiopian security activities with federal priorities, improve continuity between bilateral cooperation and AUSSOM, and give Somali authorities greater influence over the regional response to threats within their jurisdiction. As Somalia assumes greater responsibility for its own security amid uncertainty over international support, the quality of its coordination with Ethiopia will directly affect its capacity to manage cross-border threats and sustain security across its western regions. ethiopia.summary: The Sodere Initiative, launched by Ethiopia in late 1996, aimed to unify Somalia's rival factions during a period of political fragmentation following the collapse of the Somali state in 1991. Convened under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the talks led to the establishment of a 41-member National Salvation Council, representing major clan families and smaller communities. While the initiative did not create a lasting government, it laid the groundwork for future reconciliation efforts by promoting clan-family parity in political representation. Ethiopia's involvement was driven by security concerns, particularly regarding the Islamist group Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya, which posed threats to its border. The initiative's legacy continues to influence Somalia's ongoing security challenges, particularly in light of Al-Shabaab's presence and the need for coordinated regional security efforts as Somalia transitions towards greater self-governance.

ethiopia.content: The Ethiopia-Djibouti Trade Corridor and the Shared Stakes of Regional Security – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 The Ethiopia-Djibouti Trade Corridor and the Shared Stakes of Regional Security 0 Comments The TPLF-Shabiya attempt to cut the Ethiopia-Djibouti trade corridor was more than a threat to Ethiopia’s economic lifeline; it also endangered Djibouti’s economic interests. A strategy designed to pressure the Ethiopian federal government by disrupting this vital trade route would have imposed costs on both countries, potentially extending Ethiopia’s conflict into a wider regional economic crisis. The corridor is not simply a transport link between two neighbouring states. It underpins Ethiopia’s access to international markets and Djibouti’s role as a principal gateway for Ethiopian trade. More than 95 per cent of Ethiopia’s import-export trade uses the Ethio-Djibouti corridor, while Djibouti’s economy relies heavily on Ethiopian trade through its port. A disruption would have threatened Ethiopia’s access to international markets while putting Djibouti’s port-related economic activity at risk. The scale of the impact would depend on the duration and extent of the disruption, but the corridor’s importance makes its security a shared economic concern. The plan must also be understood in the context of the military imbalance between the ENDF and the opposing forces. Given the ENDF’s apparent military superiority in conventional capabilities, direct confrontation with the Ethiopian military would have presented a significant challenge. Threatening the Ethio-Djibouti corridor could have offered the opposing forces an asymmetric means of exerting pressure on the federal government. This reflects a broader strategic logic: actors facing disadvantages in direct military confrontation may seek leverage by threatening infrastructure essential to a state’s economic functioning. The corridor represented precisely such a vulnerability. However, this strategic logic alone does not establish that a coordinated plan existed; that allegation must be assessed against the reported intelligence and subsequent battlefield developments. The corridor’s strategic significance also creates a constraint for any actor seeking to exploit it. Although disruption could impose economic costs on Ethiopia, it could simultaneously undermine Djibouti’s port revenues and commercial activity, potentially broadening opposition to the threat beyond Ethiopia’s borders. Such an outcome would risk turning an attempt to pressure the Ethiopian federal government into a wider regional security concern. The interdependence of the two economies therefore has a strategic dimension: the corridor’s vulnerability is not exclusively Ethiopia’s weakness, but also a source of shared interest in preventing its disruption. This makes the protection of the route relevant to regional stability as well as bilateral economic security. The leaked intelligence report suggests that Eritrean troops were present at 50 locations in Ethiopian territory across eastern Tigray and northern Afar before the Ethiopian government launched its defensive operation. According to the report, the deployment was intended to facilitate an attempt to cut the Ethio-Djibouti trade corridor. Subsequent reporting documented the TPLF-led forces’ advance into Afar, including the capture of Erebti and their movement towards Afdeera, underscoring the region’s strategic importance to Ethiopia’s access to Djibouti. These developments provide relevant context for assessing the alleged plan, although the reported troop deployments and rebel advances do not, on their own, establish that all the actors involved were coordinating towards that objective. The presence of Eritrean troops at these locations did not, in itself, guarantee control of the corridor. On 1 October 2026, federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force units counterattacked and retook both towns, reversing much of the rebel advance in Afar. The ENDF’s technological capabilities, intelligence-gathering capacity and operational reach may have contributed to its response, although the extent of their influence cannot be established from the reported battlefield outcome alone. Further evidence concerning force coordination, operational decisions and battlefield performance would be needed to determine the precise factors behind the reversal. The counteroffensive addressed the immediate battlefield situation, but it did not eliminate the broader security concern raised by the alleged plan. The intelligence report therefore raises questions about foreign military deployments near strategically sensitive areas and the potential threats they could pose to Ethiopia’s economic security. The episode underscored the importance of integrating critical transport infrastructure into national defence planning, intelligence collection and inter-agency coordination. Protecting the Ethio-Djibouti corridor requires identifying vulnerabilities before armed actors can exploit them, as well as maintaining the capacity to respond effectively to emerging threats. Its geographic exposure and economic importance make early warning and infrastructure resilience essential components of corridor security. Djibouti’s position is central to this assessment. Ethiopia should therefore approach corridor protection as a shared bilateral concern rather than solely as a domestic security matter. Structured cooperation could help both countries exchange relevant threat assessments, coordinate security planning and safeguard the trade relationship on which their mutual economic interests depend. At the national level, Ethiopia should make corridor security a permanent national-security priority through complementary measures. Coordinated military and intelligence planning should strengthen strategic warning and enable authorities to assess credible indications of armed movements towards corridor-adjacent areas, suspicious troop deployments and attempts to disrupt transport networks. Layered protection should improve the resilience of critical transport and logistics infrastructure, reducing the risk that disruption at a single point could interrupt the wider trade route. Periodic reviews of security conditions and corridor vulnerabilities would help ensure that these measures remain responsive to changing threats. The security of the Ethiopia-Djibouti trade corridor is inseparable from the strategic interests of both countries. Although the ENDF’s reported counteroffensive reversed rebel gains in Afar, the alleged plan and the reported Eritrean troop deployments warrant further scrutiny. Preventing future threats requires sustained defence preparedness, effective early warning and institutionalised bilateral security cooperation. Ultimately, safeguarding the corridor is essential to Ethiopia’s economic security, Djibouti’s commercial interests and regional stability. Recent tensions, particularly the TPLF-Shabiya's attempts to disrupt this corridor, pose risks not only to Ethiopia's economic stability but also to Djibouti's port revenues. The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) has shown military superiority, yet threats to the corridor highlight vulnerabilities that could be exploited by opposing forces. The situation underscores the need for enhanced bilateral security cooperation and integrated defense strategies to protect this vital infrastructure. Recent military developments, including the ENDF's counteroffensive, have temporarily reversed rebel advances, but ongoing vigilance and coordinated efforts are essential to ensure the corridor's security and maintain regional stability.

ethiopia.content: Except War, What Option is Ethiopia Left With to Defend Persistent Incursions from Eritrea? – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Except War, What Option is Ethiopia Left With to Defend Persistent Incursions from Eritrea? 0 Comments Having learned from the devastating costs of the 1998 border war between Ethiopia and Eritrea and the 2020 northern Ethiopia conflict, preventing a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea remains crucial. In a region plagued by persistent conflict, militant activities, and extremist and terrorist havens, the last thing it needs is another war. As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated , “the last thing the world needs right now is another war.” However, Ethiopia’s relationship with Eritrea does not seem likely to be resolved through conventional diplomatic assurances alone. Since its secession, Eritrea has adopted an antagonistic posture toward its largest neighbor and pursued policies that challenge Ethiopia’s security and regional interests. It has a documented record of supporting anti-Ethiopian government armed groups, providing them with sanctuary and other forms of assistance. Following the Pretoria peace agreement, although Eritrean forces withdrew from Tigray’s heartland, they remained in territories inside Tigray near the Eritrean border. Eritrea also established an alliance with the TPLF and other armed groups inside Ethiopian territory, with the latter forming an alliance aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian federal government. In this context, Eritrea plays a significant role, while other external actors also contribute by providing support. The nature of the Eritrean state under the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ) remains a persistent source of insecurity for Ethiopia. The country’s political system is highly centralized and militarized, with indefinite national service, the dominance of military institutions over civilian administration, and the concentration of power in President Isaias Afwerki and his close circle all playing a central role in keeping the regime in power. Since the 1998–2000 border war, Eritrea has maintained a security posture shaped by permanent mobilization and a deep suspicion of Ethiopia. This reflects what can be described as a small-state syndrome, in which the perceived vulnerability of a state, its limited strategic depth, and its exposure to stronger neighbors shape how its leadership understands external threats. In Eritrea’s case, this outlook has reinforced the tendency to view Ethiopia through a security lens and to treat the preservation of regime security as a national priority. This reinforces the need to address the underlying strategic calculations that shape Eritrea’s behavior toward Ethiopia. In recent years, the practical consequences of this structure have become evident in Eritrea’s military presence in border areas of northern Ethiopia and its cultivation of relationships with armed groups operating inside Ethiopian territory. For more than a year, Ethiopian authorities documented patterns of material support, including ammunition intercepts and alleged training linkages, directed toward elements of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and other armed groups in Ethiopia. These activities culminated in formal Ethiopian notifications to the United Nations Security Council in October 2026, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter on the inherent right of self-defense in response to the advances of Eritrean units tens of kilometers into Tigrayan territory and coordination with domestic insurgent coalitions. The severing of diplomatic relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara in early October further removed remaining formal channels for crisis management. In this environment, Eritrea’s conduct has shifted from wartime alliance against the TPLF during 2020–2022 to a tactical realignment that treats a weakened or fragmented Ethiopian center as preferable to a consolidated neighbor capable of projecting power in the region. The nature of the regime, shaped by President Isaias Afwerki’s personalized style of rule and his longstanding political outlook towards Ethiopia, makes it unlikely that Asmara will voluntarily provide the guarantees necessary for de-escalation. For Ethiopia, however, Isaias’s decades-long rule has remained a persistent security concern, given Eritrea’s history of hostility towards its southern neighbor and its support for armed with anti-government agendas. Ethiopia needs credible guarantees from Eritrea to address these concerns, ease tensions, and create conditions for a lasting resolution. However, as noted above, the nature of Eritrea’s leadership makes such guarantees difficult to secure, particularly if they require a change in the security policies and political outlook that have shaped its approach towards Ethiopia for decades. Demands for an end to support for armed opposition groups, the cessation of cross-border arms transfers, and a verifiable halt to military preparations near Ethiopian territory would require the Eritrean leadership to reconsider practices closely tied to its system of internal control. Introduced during the 1998–2000 border war, national service has evolved into an indefinite obligation serving both military and labor needs. Many Eritreans remain in service for years, often with little control over their assignments and limited remuneration. Its prolonged nature also gives the government considerable influence over citizens’ livelihoods and their ability to leave state service. In Eritrea, generals often wield greater authority than civilian officials at the zonal level, with power ultimately concentrated in the presidency. Isaias Afwerki has also rotated military commanders and senior officials, limiting their ability to build independent power bases. Control over the economy, political coordination, information, and national security remains concentrated among a small circle of trusted figures whose influence depends heavily on their relationship with the president. Under such conditions, transparency and demobilization would be perceived as a threat to the regime’s capacity to extract resources, suppress dissent, and justify isolation. The empirical record of Eritrean foreign policy since its secession, marked by disputes with Yemen, Djibouti, Sudan, and Ethiopia, illustrates a consistent preference for confrontation over institutionalized cooperation when the latter would constrain personalist authority. In essence, full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would risk repeating the cost of the previous conflicts, while increasing the risk of regional actors becoming involved. A direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would be an uneven contest given Ethiopia’s demographic and military scale. Yet Eritrea’s garrison-state structure would allow it to mobilize much of its population and national resources with potentially devastating consequences for its population and economy. Therefore, Ethiopia’s dilemma would be how to neutralize the threat posed by Eritrea’s leadership without turning the military imbalance into a prolonged and costly conflict. Given these constraints, effective threat neutralization begins with identifying the specific sources of risk. These include Eritrea’s military presence, support for armed groups, and other activities directed by its leadership that threaten Ethiopia’s security. Given the concentration of political and security authority within Eritrea’s leadership, a surgical and swift operation directed at the narrow decision-making and security core offers a theoretically coherent pathway. The personalist character of the Eritrean system concentrates operational and political authority in a limited set of individuals and institutions surrounding the president. However, this approach would require a carefully defined communication strategy to establish the basis for action, build international understanding of its security concerns and demonstrate that any measures taken are necessary and proportionate to the threats identified. Israel’s approach towards Iran illustrates how operations targeting senior leadership and key decision-making structures can disrupt command arrangements and weaken a state’s capacity to coordinate its response. However, Iran’s institutional depth has allowed it to sustain resistance despite the loss of senior figures. Eritrea differs in this respect, but the case provides an illustration. Its political system is more personalized, with authority concentrated around Isaias Afwerki and a narrow circle of military and security officials. Let alone the removal of the inner circle, the removal of Isaias would be consequential extending beyond Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns, potentially reshaping Eritrea’s political order and the wider Horn of Africa. Eritrea’s relatively shallow administrative depth, compared with more layered systems that possess provincial redundancy or institutionalized revolutionary guards, may increase the disruptive potential of precise action against the center. For international actors, Eritrea’s status as a pariah state, its record of playing a spoiler role in the region, and its government’s persistent human rights violations would shape how they assess such a development. The prospect of a change in leadership could be viewed as an opportunity to address longstanding sources of regional instability and the country’s human rights crisis. In its 2015 report, the UN Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea found that “systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations have been and are being committed in Eritrea under the authority of the Government,” adding that some of these violations “may constitute crimes against humanity.” Beyond this, such an approach could help avert a devastating interstate war, free the Eritrean people from a tyrannical and deeply oppressive regime and minimize wider humanitarian consequences. The broader regional context reinforces the logic of limitation. A major war would intersect with ongoing conflicts in Sudan, competition over Red Sea access, and Nile water disputes, creating opportunities for external actors to deeply embed themselves in the region. Eritrea’s alignment with SAF’s al-Burhan and Egypt mean that uncontrolled escalation would quickly expand the geographic and political scope of the conflict. By contrast, a tightly constrained operation that demonstrably prioritizes the neutralization of leadership-directed threats minimizes the grounds for third-party intervention and preserves Ethiopia’s capacity to address internal security challenges. The small-state syndrome that shapes Eritrean behavior is characterized by acute sensitivity to Ethiopia’s growing regional role and influence, alongside a tendency to use asymmetric means to constrain Ethiopia’s position and establish strategic buffer zones along its borders including through support for the TPLF. As noted, Eritrea’s political and security system is built around military mobilization, secrecy, and the use of regional networks to advance its strategic interests. For Ethiopia to achieve lasting security, Eritrea would need to provide credible assurances against military build-up, arms trafficking, and support for proxy groups, including the TPLF and other armed movements, while preventing its territory from being used as a sanctuary for groups seeking to destabilize Ethiopia. However, the centralized and highly personalized nature of Isaias Afwerki’s rule raises serious doubts about whether such commitments would be honored without meaningful pressure. Ethiopia’s long-term security interests therefore depend on addressing these sources of interference while avoiding the heavy costs of a prolonged interstate war. A carefully considered approach, supported by verified intelligence and a coherent communication strategy, seeks to address immediate security threats while preserving the prospects for long-term regional stability. Ethiopia cannot afford to remain trapped in the same recurring cycle of confrontation with Eritrea, in which unresolved threats repeatedly generate new tensions and bring both countries closer to a devastating war. The 1998 border war and the 2020 conflict in northern Ethiopia highlight the devastating costs of war, making conflict avoidance crucial. Eritrea's support for anti-Ethiopian armed groups and its military presence near the border exacerbate tensions. Diplomatic efforts have faltered, particularly after the severing of relations in October 2026. Ethiopia's challenge lies in neutralizing Eritrea's threats without escalating to full-scale war, which could draw in regional actors and have catastrophic consequences. A targeted approach against Eritrean leadership may offer a pathway to mitigate risks while avoiding broader conflict, emphasizing the need for international understanding and support to address these security concerns effectively.

Opening the three-day capacity development workshop today, Ethiopia's Auditor General Meseret Damtie said strengthening African Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) is essential in order to promote accountable governance, sound public financial management and sustainable development across the continent. She emphasized that improved audit quality, institutional capacity and collaboration are essential to enable audit institutions fulfil their mandates effectively. "At the heart of ARISE (African Regional Initiative for Strengthening Effectiveness) is the spirit of peer support and collaboration," the Auditor General said, highlighting the importance of cooperation among participating institutions, programme coordinators, peer SAIs and development partners in achieving sustainable results. Meseret linked the principles of cooperation and collective responsibility underpinning ARISE to Ethiopia's Medemer philosophy, which emphasizes synergy, shared contributions and common goals. She highlighted the importance of collaboration in strengthening institutions and advancing sustainable development, reflecting the program's emphasis on partnerships and collective efforts to improve public-sector accountability across Africa. INTOSAI Development Initiative (IDI) representative, Muhammed Dabo, stressed that sustainable improvements in Supreme Audit Institutions require more than technical training, emphasizing strong institutional systems, effective leadership, capable personnel and the ability to manage change. "Each partner has a distinct role, but we share one objective: stronger, more effective and sustainable Supreme Audit Institutions," he said, underscoring the complementary roles of beneficiary SAIs, peer institutions, regional organizations and development partners. Dabo encouraged the participants to share experiences openly, identify challenges early, adapt when necessary and develop practical solutions for their respective institutions. He stressed that the workshop's success should be measured by the lessons applied and improvements achieved after participants return to their work. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: TPLF Had Been Preparing for War - PM Abiy - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: TPLF Had Been Preparing for War - PM Abiy 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The defunct TPLF had been preparing for another round of war, violating the Pretoria Agreement, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed revealed. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), he said the TPLF violated the Pretoria Agreement signed in October 2022. The PM recalled that the key elements of the Pretoria Agreement included cessation of hostilities, restoration of all services, disarmament, return of displaced people, and recognition of the constitutional order. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The federal government had fulfilled everything that was possible and expected of it, he added. On the contrary, the TPLF had been purchasing and soliciting weapons as well as openly recruiting young people instead of implementing the agreement to disarm combatants. Above all, PM Abiy pointed out that after the agreement, the TPLF used displaced persons as hostages to prevent them from returning to their homes. Additionally, it engaged in destroying and closing down infrastructure--including airlines, banking, and telecommunications--that had been restored by the Federal Government to deliver services. Despite the group's misdeeds, the PM stated that the government had forewarned that war was not worthwhile and that peace was preferable. However, the TPLF disregarded the advice and collaborated with various forces, and violated the Pretoria Agreement by initiating an unnecessary war. Immense damage has been inflicted on the public as a result of the war instigated by the TPLF, he noted. War is bad and yields no benefit, the Premier further noted, adding that a war fought for the interests of foreign forces is even worse. The psychological damage is not to be taken lightly and damage has also been inflicted on development and the economy. PM Abiy stressed that young people carrying Kalashnikovs should therefore return to work and participate in the development and rehabilitation of Tigray. Noting that many young people were forcibly recruited, he advised those who have not yet returned to return to normal life. He stated that the leaders of the TPLF have been declaring war for 50 years without dying or being wounded themselves; instead they sent their children and families abroad and to Addis Ababa where they are engaged in business and construction. Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people," he said. The two countries also cooperate in regional security, cross-border infrastructure, trade, telecommunications, and electricity interconnections, supporting economic integration and development across the Horn of Africa, it was learned. The memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed Saturday in Mogadishu by Transport and Civil Aviation Minister Mohamed Farah Nuh, Somali Civil Aviation Authority Director General Ahmed Moallim Hassan and Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s regional vice president for Africa and the Middle East. advertisements Under the agreement, the Somali Civil Aviation Authority will recognize the IATA Operational Safety Audit (IOSA) and the IATA Safety Audit for Ground Operations (ISAGO) as acceptable means of compliance with national regulations, complementing its own safety oversight functions. The programs will complement, rather than replace, the authority’s own regulatory and safety oversight functions. “Global safety standards are the cornerstone of efficient and safe operations. Through this MoU, we will work with the Somali CAA towards the continuous improvement of safety standards, promote the adoption of industry best practices, and foster a culture of safety across the aviation sector. This partnership reflects our mutual dedication to advancing aviation safety for the benefit of passengers, operators and the wider aviation industry in Somalia and Africa,” said Kamil Alawadhi, IATA’s Regional Vice President for Africa and Middle East. IOSA is an internationally recognized audit system designed to assess an airline’s operational management and control systems. More than 450 airlines are currently listed on the IOSA registry, and all IATA member airlines are required to maintain IOSA registration. ISAGO applies similar standardized oversight to companies providing ground-handling services at airports. IATA says the program is intended to reduce operational risks, improve consistency in ground handling and limit duplication between audits conducted by airlines, airports and regulators. The agreement forms part of IATA’s Focus Africa initiative, which includes efforts to improve aviation safety, infrastructure, connectivity and regulatory standards across the continent. The agreement signed in Mogadishu comes as authorities continue rebuilding a civil aviation system that was severely weakened after the collapse of the central government in 1991. The country has gradually reestablished national control over aviation functions, including management of Somali airspace and regulatory oversight of airlines and airports.
